lesson.title: Reaganomics: Tax Cuts, Deregulation, and the Supply-Side Gamble
lesson.summary: Reagan's economic program, often called Reaganomics, bet that cutting tax rates and regulation would unleash enough new investment and growth to lift the whole economy, a theory that produced both a deep early recession and a long recovery, along with a much larger federal debt.
lesson.body:
The economic theory behind Reaganomics is usually called supply side economics, because it focused on increasing the supply of goods and services in the economy by giving businesses and investors stronger incentives to produce, rather than on boosting demand through government spending, which had been the more common approach since the New Deal. A key idea, popularized by economist Arthur Laffer and often illustrated with what became known as the Laffer Curve, held that tax rates could in some cases be so high that cutting them would actually increase government revenue over time, by encouraging more work, investment, and economic activity. Not all economists accepted this claim, and even Reagan's eventual vice president, George H.W. Bush, had famously dismissed the idea as voodoo economics while running against Reagan in the 1980 Republican primaries.

Congress passed the centerpiece of Reagan's program, the Economic Recovery Tax Act, in 1981, which cut the top marginal income tax rate from 70 percent to 50 percent and reduced rates across other income brackets as well. The administration paired the tax cuts with a push to reduce federal regulation on industries like energy, transportation, and finance, arguing that regulatory costs were holding back business investment. At the same time, Reagan sharply increased defense spending as part of his broader Cold War strategy, even as he sought, with only partial success, to cut non defense domestic spending.

In the short run, the economy went through a severe recession in 1981 and 1982, driven largely by the Federal Reserve under chairman Paul Volcker, who kept interest rates very high to finally break the inflation of the 1970s. Unemployment rose above 10 percent, and Reagan's approval ratings fell along with it. Once inflation came down, though, the economy entered a long recovery beginning in late 1982 and 1983, with strong growth for the rest of the decade, and Reagan's supporters pointed to that recovery as proof the tax cuts had worked.

The recovery came with a major cost. Because tax revenues fell more than spending was cut, especially with defense spending rising sharply, the federal deficit and the national debt grew enormously during Reagan's presidency, with the debt roughly tripling over the course of the 1980s. Critics argued this proved supply side theory's revenue promises had failed, while supporters argued the tax cuts and defense buildup were worth the cost, and this basic disagreement over Reaganomics has continued to shape American political debate over taxes and spending ever since.
